newsitem.title: INDIA: Feeble signs of rise in Indian bank credit offtake.
newsitem.headline: Feeble signs of rise in Indian bank credit offtake.

text.p: Indian banks' credit offtake is showing feeble signs of an uptrend but real growth in credit demand may have to wait till September or October, bankers said.
Banks' non-food credit growth edged up marginally to 12.4 percent on May 23 year-on-year from 12.1 percent two weeks ago, according to the latest Reserve Bank of India (RBI) figures.
"There is a slight year-on-year growth, but it has fallen by 21.59 billion rupees to 2,681.05 billion rupees on May 23 compared to May 9 figures," said an analyst at a research firm.
"The supply side is bright -- interest rates are down, liquidity is good, but government spending is down," she said.

"The government has cut down spending to achieve its 1997/98 target of fiscal deficit at 4.5 percent (of GDP) from 5.0 percent. This has not been compensated for by rise in private sector investment or consumption," the analyst said.
On the external side, exports were decelerating because of a global trade slump and an overvalued rupee hurting Indian competitiveness, analysts said.
Some bankers said they saw signs of credit picking up.
"Credit is picking up, especially foreign currency loans," said R. Nagarajan, general manager at Bank of India, one of India's leading state-run banks.
"We get the feeling rupee loans are also picking up."
An economist said the RBI figures may be understated because banks are increasingly lending to firms by subscribing to their debentures and preference shares.
"These go to meet working capital needs but don't get reflected in the RBI data," he said.

He called it a structural shift in bank lending prompted partly by the fact that subscriptions to debentures and the like do not have to be matched by lending to "non-priority" sectors in rural areas where loan recovery has been a problem.
Banks in India have to mandatorily lend a portion of their total loans for agriculture and other "priority" sectors.
"Corporate sentiments are upbeat compared to six months ago. Demand for some commodities like steel are picking up," he said.
While opinions differ on whether a slowdown in industry has been reversed, there is a near consensus that the second half of 1997/98 (April-March) will see a turnaround.
"I see a recovery after September," said an analyst.
He said good monsoon rains for the 10th successive year followed by a good harvest and the onset of Diwali festival will fuel demand across the countryside, triggering an industrial revival.
Year-on-year industrial growth as measured by the index for industrial production slowed to 7.0 percent during April 1996 to February 1997, the government said last week.
The index grew at 11.8 percent during the year-ago period.
